subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Show that the four points in the Argand plane represented by the complex numbers 2 + i, 4 + 3i, 2 + 5i, 3i are the vertices of a square.

mark_split.label: Write the four points and the distance formula
Find the four sides and the two diagonals
State equal sides, equal diagonals, and conclude

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.48 — SAQ chapter 7 Complex Numbers, answer 54.2. (Book page = PDF page − 1 in this part of the scan.) The chapter header carries ★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that ★★ is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. recall_prompt: Say how you would show that the four points make a square — what you compute, how many distances there are, and what two facts you need at the end.
insider_note: Six distances, not four — equal sides alone only prove a rhombus, so the two diagonals must also be computed and shown equal. And read 3i as the point (0, 3): taking it as (3, 0) breaks every distance that uses D.

steps.label: Write the points
steps.margin_note: First mark. Note that 3i is 0 + 3i, the point (0, 3) — the missing real part is where this question is most often lost. Write the four points in the order given; that order is the order round the square.

recall.must_convey: That the four complex numbers are taken as the points A(2, 1), B(4, 3), C(2, 5), D(0, 3) — with 3i as (0, 3) — and that the distance formula gives the lengths.
accept: write the four numbers as points and note that three i is zero comma three
the points are two one, four three, two five and zero three
take real and imaginary parts as x and y for all four points
naalugu complex numbers ni points ga rayali, three i ante zero comma three
convert each number to a point then use the distance formula

steps.why: A square is a coordinate-geometry fact: four equal sides and two equal diagonals. Turning the four numbers into four points is the only place the complex numbers are used; everything after is distances.
common_mistakes: Reading 3i as the point (3, 0) instead of (0, 3).
Taking the points in a different order from the question, so the 'sides' computed are actually diagonals.
Never writing the distance formula and then dropping a square inside the root.

steps.label: Sketch the square
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark. The square stands on the corner A, so its diagonals AC and BD (dashed) are vertical and horizontal — that is why they come out as whole numbers, 4 and 4.

recall.must_convey: That the four points are marked on the Argand plane, joined in order A B C D, and both diagonals drawn. Naming the sketch is full credit.
accept: draw the four points and join them in order with both diagonals
sketch A B C D on the axes and draw A C and B D
mark the four points and draw the square with its diagonals
naalugu points guruthu pettukoni square geesi diagonals geeyali
plot and join the points, then the two diagonals

steps.why: The sketch fixes which pairs are sides (AB, BC, CD, DA) and which are diagonals (AC, BD). Without it a student often computes AC as a side and 'proves' the sides unequal.
common_mistakes: Joining A to C as a side.
Drawing the square with sides parallel to the axes — this one is tilted 45°.

elements.caption: Step 2 — the four sides AB, BC, CD, DA
Step 3 — the two diagonals AC and BD

steps.label: Find sides and diagonals
steps.margin_note: Half the marks, six short distances. Every side is √8 and every diagonal is √16 = 4. Do all six — four equal sides alone would only show a rhombus.

recall.must_convey: That the four sides AB, BC, CD, DA each come to √8 and the two diagonals AC, BD each come to 4, all by the distance formula.
accept: the four sides are each root eight and the two diagonals are each four
compute A B, B C, C D, D A which are all root eight and A C, B D which are both four
all four sides equal root eight and both diagonals equal four
naalugu sides root eight, rendu diagonals four vasthai
six distances, sides root eight, diagonals four

steps.why: A square needs two facts, not one: equal sides (which a rhombus also has) and equal diagonals (which only a rectangle or square has). Both together force a square, so both sets of distances are part of the proof.
common_mistakes: Stopping after the four sides — that proves only a rhombus.
Computing AC and BD as sides and reporting 'the sides are not equal'.
Writing √8 as 2√2 in some lines and √8 in others, then doubting they are equal.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Two sentences: sides equal, diagonals equal. Then name the shape.
lines: AB = BC = CD = DA = √8 — the four sides are equal.
AC = BD = 4 — the two diagonals are equal.

lines.text: ∴ A, B, C, D form a square.

recall.must_convey: That equal sides together with equal diagonals make ABCD a square.
accept: four equal sides and two equal diagonals so A B C D is a square
sides are equal and diagonals are equal therefore it is a square
since all sides match and both diagonals match the figure is a square
sides equal, diagonals equal kabatti square
equal sides plus equal diagonals means square

steps.why: The conclusion has to name both facts because the question is 'show that'. A rhombus with unequal diagonals (the next question in this chapter) fails the second test — writing both lines is what separates the two answers.
common_mistakes: Ending on the last distance with no sentence.
